references.text: The parallel account in Mark where Jesus threatens the unclean spirit and commands it to come out. Here too, the spirit throws the man down before coming out, but without harming him.
Jesus threatened the demons and did not allow them to speak, reflecting his authority over evil spirits and his command for them to be silent.
The unclean spirits fell down before Jesus and cried out who he was, but Jesus strictly forbade them from making him known – the same pattern of silencing demons.
Here too, Jesus drives out demons that cry out that he is the Son of God; he threatens them and forbids them to speak because they knew he was the Christ.
Another incident where a demon throws a person down (ῥίψαν), but Jesus threatens the unclean spirit, heals the boy, and gives him back to his father.
Jesus commands the unclean spirit to come out of the man, showing the same sovereign authority over demons as in Luke 4:35.

Jesus threatens an unclean spirit and commands it to come out and never enter again. The spirit screamed and convulsed violently in the boy before coming out – parallel to the demon throwing the man down in Luke 4:35.
The disciples rejoice that demons are obedient to them in Jesus' name, and Jesus confirms his power over Satan – already demonstrated in Luke 4:35.
Paul commands a spirit to come out in the name of Jesus Christ, following the pattern of Jesus' own exorcism where he drives out the evil spirit with a single word.
Jesus commands the unclean spirit to come out of the man. Here too, the demon's violent impact on the person is described, but Jesus shows complete mastery.
